Rom-coms for the last days of summer

Hi, friend!

Summer may be winding down, but there’s still time to claim a few more sunny afternoons with a good story. We’re filling the beach bag with witty romances, destination weddings, and colorful resorts. Whether you’re heading to the shore or staying close to home, these books, movies, and shows will keep the summer vibes going a little longer.

Books to Pack Before Summer Ends

One Golden Summer

by Carley Fortune

Alice takes her grandmother back to the lake cottage where they once spent an unforgettable summer. There she reconnects with Charlie and recruits him to help complete her summer bucket list. Days on the water, creative sparks, and an increasingly hard-to-ignore attraction follow.

The Hotel Nantucket

by Elin Hilderbrand

After a major renovation, the Hotel Nantucket is ready for a comeback. New GM Lizbet must rally an eccentric staff and demanding guests—all while the ghost of a former chambermaid watches from the halls. This lively ensemble story mixes island vibes, workplace comedy, and romance.

Sun, Schemes & Poolside Comedy

Palm Royale

Streaming on Apple TV

In 1969 Palm Beach, determined outsider Maxine will try almost anything to secure a place among the town’s richest residents. Kristen Wiig leads a star-filled cast through country-club rivalries, elaborate outfits, and increasingly outrageous social schemes.

Acapulco

Streaming on Apple TV

Young Máximo lands his dream job at Acapulco’s most glamorous resort in the 1980s, only to discover that keeping guests happy is far more complicated than he imagined. Between demanding visitors, workplace mishaps, family obligations, and romantic detours, his new career becomes a brightly colored comedy of errors.

20 Novels with Immaculate Beachy Vibes

Destination-Wedding Rom-Coms

Ticket to Paradise

Streaming on Netflix

George Clooney and Julia Roberts play divorced parents who travel to Bali with a shared mission: stop their daughter’s wedding. Their plan quickly unearths old arguments and signs that their own story may not be finished. The result is a wanderlust-filled, breezy second-chance comedy.

Anyone But You

Streaming on Hulu

After their first date goes spectacularly wrong, Bea and Ben are reunited at a destination wedding in Australia. To make the weekend easier—or possibly much more complicated—they agree to pretend they’re a couple. Sydney Sweeney and Glen Powell bring the chemistry and chaos, while coastal views does the rest.

Cozy stories for slowing down

Hi, friend!

September often arrives with packed calendars and a fresh push to get more done. With self-care in focus this month, we’re turning to stories that make space for slower days—from a traveling tea monk and a Tokyo bookshop to handwritten poems. These warm picks show us how much we can discover when we slow down and take notice.

Books That Take Their Time

These books aren’t in a hurry. Settle in with two loveable characters who step away from their usual day-to-day and begin to rethink what they really want out of life.

A Psalm for the Wild-Built

by Becky Chambers

Sibling Dex leaves the city and becomes a traveling tea monk, serving warm drinks and listening to people talk about their problems. Their quiet journey takes an unexpected turn when Mosscap, a curious robot returning to human society after centuries, arrives with one big question: What do people need? This hopeful, cozy science-fiction story has plenty to say about rest, purpose, and the pressure to always want more.

Days at the Morisaki Bookshop

by Satoshi Yagisawa

After a breakup turns her life upside down, Takako leaves her job and moves into the tiny room above her uncle’s secondhand bookshop in Tokyo. Her days become filled with sleep, stacks of books, neighborhood cafés, and conversations with her eccentric uncle. Slowly, the bookshop helps her reconnect with the world and imagine what might come next.

Embracing the Ordinary

These picks find their rhythm in familiar routines and characters who discover that a full life doesn’t have to be a constantly busy one.

Perfect Days

Available to rent

Hirayama spends his days cleaning public restrooms in Tokyo and his free time listening to cassette tapes, reading, photographing trees, and enjoying familiar neighborhood spots. His quiet routine becomes the heart of this warm, observant film, which finds richness in an ordinary day and shows how much life opens up when every moment isn’t rushed.

Paterson

Streaming on Prime Video

Adam Driver is a New Jersey bus driver and poet whose days follow a familiar rhythm: driving his route, writing in his notebook, walking his dog, and stopping at the neighborhood bar. Rather than chasing a dramatic transformation, the film finds humor and beauty in the ordinary, quiet creativity, and paying attention to the life already unfolding around you.

Escaping the Grind

A Good Year

Max Skinner is a hard-charging London banker who inherits the Provençal vineyard where he spent childhood summers with his uncle. He plans to sell it quickly, but the sunshine, wine, familiar memories, and an unexpected romance begin to interfere with his schedule. Russell Crowe stars in this scenic escape about trading a life ruled by work for one with a little more flavor.

School is back in session (for everyone!)

Hi, friend!

Backpacks are packed, and classrooms are filling up, but learning doesn’t have an age limit. Today’s picks follow people who head back to school, try something unfamiliar, and form new connections along the way. You may even come away ready to take a class, pick up a book, or finally try that hobby you’ve been thinking about.

It’s Never Too Late

Starting from scratch can feel awkward, especially when we’re used to knowing what we’re doing. These picks celebrate the fun, frustration, and satisfaction of beginning again.

Beginners

by Tom Vanderbilt

Inspired by his daughter’s endless curiosity, journalist Tom Vanderbilt spends a year learning new skills simply because he wants to. From singing and drawing to juggling and surfing, his adventures explore why adults often stop trying unfamiliar things—and what we can gain by being willing to look like a beginner again.

The First Grader

Available to rent

Based on a true story, this inspiring film follows Kimani Maruge, an 84-year-old Kenyan man who finally gets the chance to pursue the education he was denied. When free primary schooling becomes available, he arrives at his local school ready to learn to read, even if it means sharing a classroom with six-year-olds.

Starting Again Spotlight

The Intern

Retirement isn’t keeping 70-year-old widower Ben Whittaker busy, so he applies to become a senior intern at a fast-growing online fashion company. As Ben learns his way around a new workplace, his younger coworkers discover that he has plenty to teach them, too. Robert De Niro and Anne Hathaway star in this warm comedy about staying curious, adapting to change, and bringing different generations together.

What We Learn From Each Other

Some of the best lessons never appear on a syllabus. These stories show how teachers, friends, and even strangers can help us see things differently.

Abbott Elementary

Streaming on Hulu

The students aren’t the only ones learning at this underfunded Philadelphia public school. Janine, Barbara, Gregory, Melissa, Jacob, and their unpredictable principal, Ava, regularly improvise their way through classroom challenges while learning from their mistakes and each other. It’s a funny, bighearted salute to the people who keep showing up for their students.

The Reading List

by Sara Nisha Adams

Teenage library worker Aleisha discovers a handwritten list of novels tucked inside a returned book and decides to read every title. When recently widowed Mukesh visits the library hoping to connect with his book-loving granddaughter, the list brings the two strangers together and opens a new chapter for them both.

Creator Spotlight

“I Tried to Learn Tennis in 30 Days, this is what happened”

Watch Makari Espe try, and fail, and try again through many different activities on YouTube. From biking, surfing, tennis, and even a triathlon. Her goal? Push through the discomfort and feel the joy of being a beginner at something new!

The top 10 TV shows based on video games

Hey, friend!

Right now, the world’s biggest gaming convention, Gamescom, is underway in Cologne, Germany, bringing a wave of exciting reveals and announcements. From a first look at The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered to an extended gameplay trailer for Gears of War: E-Day, there’s plenty for gamers to be excited about.

But since most of these aren't playable yet, we're here to recommend the best content to keep you entertained until these games release. Keep reading to discover the best TV shows based on video games, the books your favorite games borrowed from, and the most anticipated video game movies on the horizon.

The Top 10 TV Shows Based on Video Games

From fungal outbreaks to nuclear wastelands, these are the ten shows that took video game source material and actually did it justice.

The Witcher

Mutated monster-hunter Geralt of Rivia struggles to find his place in a world where people often prove to be more wicked than beasts. In honor of the upcoming The Witcher 3 remaster that was just announced at Gamescom, we had to take this moment to encourage you to watch the show! It’s definitely binge-worthy.

The Books Behind Your Favorite Video Games

Here are 10 books you didn't know were the inspiration behind some of the most iconic video games.

Roadside Picnic

by Arkady and Boris Strugatsky

Red Schuhart risks his life sneaking into the Zone, a quarantined stretch of Earth where alien visitors left behind objects nobody can explain, including one rumored to grant wishes. This landmark 1972 sci-fi novel was later adapted into Andrei Tarkovsky's movie Stalker, and its fingerprints are all over the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. game franchise.

The Most Anticipated Video Game Movies

For years, video game movies were a joke. There were plenty of misfires (Super Mario Bros., Street Fighter, Max Payne) before Hollywood started taking these IPs seriously. Here are the most exciting upcoming movies based on beloved video games.

Resident Evil

In theaters September 18

Bryan (Austin Abrams) is a medical courier delivering a package to a remote hospital, until he gets caught in the middle of an outbreak and must fight through hordes of creatures to survive. Coming from the mind of Zach Cregger, (Weapons, Barbarian) fans have a lot of faith that this reboot will make people forget the disastrous 2002 movie ever existed.

posts.title: “I’ve listened to this podcast every week for the last decade”
posts.text:
“I’ve listened to this podcast every week for the last decade”

Hi, friend!

Welcome back to Insider Pix, where we uncover what entertainment and culture insiders are watching, reading, and listening to! Next up:

Claire Carusillo

Claire Carusillo is the co-owner of Storyboard, a bookstore/skate shop/coffee bar in Midway, UT. Her first novel The Responsible Party is out now, and has debuted to high praise. The New York Times calls it “A terrifically comic debut novel . . . [that] succeeds by way of its outlandish story line as much as by its singular voice.”

The Responsible Party

After police investigating a decades-old murder come looking for her mother, a disgraced influencer digs into her family’s past and uncovers the wild, tangled history of generations of women famous for surviving the impossible.

Claire’s 5 Picks

A 5-star-worthy book you’d recommend to anyone?

A Children's Bible by Lydia Millet. I don't even know anything about the Bible, and for years I haven't been able to shut up about this book. If anything, the book's guiding text is Frog and Toad. Apocalyptic, funny, and tender.

Best TV show you’ve watched recently?

I used to almost exclusively watch Housewives, but they've lost their luster to me recently. I watched all of the Vanderpump Rules spin-off The Valley with gusto, but I can hardly call that the best TV show I've watched recently, though I could probably write a 3,000-word manifesto on it if given the opportunity.

I turned to Widow's Bay earlier this summer, and I'm so glad that I did. I love a multi-generational nautical story where something ain't quite right in the water.

Best movie you’ve watched recently?

We watched Robert Redford's The Outlaw Trail documentary on YouTube where he spends three weeks riding on horseback through a historic trail with a camera crew. He wrote an accompanying book that we found at an antique mall that alerted us to the presence of the film. Red shows us ghost towns and other places in the Southwest, particularly in Utah where I live, that were already busted in 1978 and virtually non-existent now. It's a remarkable archival piece.

A hidden gem you wish more people knew about?

This Is My House, a BBC show partially available on YouTube. Five British people claiming to have the same name give a presenter a tour of a home that they all claim is theirs and theirs alone. A panel watching has to determine who is not lying.

I also loved both seasons of LOL: Last One Laughing UK. I tried to play along and not laugh during each episode and never made it far. I love Bob Mortimer!

Go-to weekly podcast?

I've listened to Hollywood Handbook every week for the last decade and change. I think the podcast's original intent was to be a send-up of insider LA comedy culture where two smart, fairly sheepish guys pretended to be dickwad know-it-alls, but it almost immediately devolved into something less conceptual. It's bizarre and ineffable but always makes me laugh and screen-record bits to send to my sister and our friend Megan.

I've been a proud Who? Weekly wholigan since Day 1. I fall asleep to back episodes of Threedom several nights a week. They're like my little friends singing me to sleep. And they're always singing.

Pix: Where did the idea for The Responsible Party first come from, and when did you realize you knew what you wanted the novel to look like? What made you choose autofiction for this novel instead of going with straight-up fiction or memoir?

“CC: As is true for the narrator "Claire Carusillo" in the book, I've been haunted since I was a child by the true story of shipwrecks and mistaken identity weathered by my great-great-grandmother Fanny Mounsey and my great-great-aunt Sarah Mounsey. Their messed-up siren song has always pulled me in, and they were always at the core of the book I wanted to write. I also knew that I was never going to be able to research my way into the exact truth of what happened to them, so I was never all that interested in writing a non-fiction book about them. In some ways, I'm too self-centered of a writer to not put myself into my work, so I always wanted to be a part of it, too.”

Pix: Who are the authors who inspire you?

“CC: Lydia Millet is my favorite author right now: she observes living through climate change and apocalyptic events as a funny person, and I hoped to emulate that end-of-the-world hum in the background of The Responsible Party. Her book A Children's Bible will continue to inspire for years to come. Ditto Miriam Toews. All My Puny Sorrows, which I wasn't introduced to until I was a graduate student in Leslie Jamison's class, changed my life. Vladimir Nabokov taught me narrators don't have to be telling the whole truth for a book to say something honest. Whenever someone comes into my bookstore Storyboard looking for a "classic," I suggest Pale Fire. Should be required reading in middle school.”

Pix: If The Responsible Party was turned into a movie or series, who would make up your dream cast?

“CC: There's a (somewhat delusional) observation by the narrator in the text that Kath, her mother, would ideally be played by Catherine O'Hara when the murder-mystery plotline got made into an in-book-universe prestige drama series. I've loved Catherine O'Hara ever since her “God Loves A Terrier” song in Best in Show, and she was taken from us too soon. The rest of my cast is stacked: Elsie Fisher from Eighth Grade as young Kath. Chris Fleming as Ron. Ivy Wolk as young Kath's best friend Marcy. Tom Schwartz from Vanderpump Rules can make his return to acting and be Irving, the aging playboy scion who lives in the lighthouse in 1971. Swoosie Kurtz from Pushing Daisies can be old Fanny and Frances McDormand can be old Sarah. The Fanning sisters made juuuust a touch homelier can be young Fanny and Sarah.”

Hey, friend!

Keep reading for the dog movies that’ll bring tears to your eyes, the books that hit differently when you have a dog, and the shows where dogs are the main characters.

Good Boys & Girls: Dog Movies That’ll Make You Cry

These heartwarming movies prove what we’ve known all along: we don’t deserve dogs.

The Art of Racing in the Rain

Aspiring race-car driver Denny (Milo Ventimiglia) navigates love, family, and unimaginable loss alongside his devoted golden retriever, Enzo, voiced by Kevin Costner. Seeing one family’s highest highs and lowest lows through their dog’s eyes makes this an especially poignant reminder of just how much our pets witness alongside us.

Books That Hit Different When You Have a Dog

Once you've loved a dog, stories about loyalty, companionship, and saying goodbye have a way of hitting you right where it hurts.

Marley & Me

by John Grogan

John Grogan's memoir about the “world's worst dog” is really about the ten unforgettable years when Marley taught him what unconditional love costs. Watching Marley grow from an unruly puppy into an irreplaceable member of the family captures all the joy—and eventual heartbreak—that makes loving a dog so bittersweet.

From heroic hounds to mischievous pups, these shows put our four-legged best friends in the spotlight.

Lassie

A remarkably clever collie helps her human companions out of one predicament after another in this family classic. She also teaches her best friend Jeff (Tommy Rettig) about love, nature and commitment. Lassie ran for nearly two decades, becoming the symbol of the quintessential loyal dog.

Incredible stories from the American Southwest

Hi, friend!

Today, we’re heading west, where red-rock canyons meet rugged peaks, and the horizon seems to stretch forever. These books, movies, and shows explore the region through thrilling mysteries, hard-won journeys, and stories rooted in the cultures and communities that call it home. Lace up your imaginary hiking boots—adventure awaits from the comfort of your couch.

7 Modern Mountain & Southwest Adventures

The Southwest is more than a spectacular backdrop in these stories. Its landscapes, histories, and communities shape every mystery, challenge, and adventure.

Dark Winds

Streaming on AMC+

Set in the 1970s, this atmospheric crime drama follows Navajo Tribal Police officers Joe Leaphorn, Jim Chee, and Bernadette Manuelito as they investigate troubling cases across Navajo Nation. Based on Tony Hillerman’s Leaphorn and Chee novels, the series combines gripping Southwestern noir with a strong sense of culture, place, and community.

Rez Ball

Streaming on Netflix

After losing their star player, the Chuska Warriors must pull together to keep their hopes of a state championship alive. Set in New Mexico and rooted in Native American culture, this uplifting underdog story captures the energy, resilience, and deep community pride surrounding Navajo basketball.

Documentary Spotlight

Unbranded

Four young cowboys adopt and train a group of wild mustangs before embarking on an epic 3,000-mile ride from the Mexican border to Canada. Crossing deserts, canyons, mountains, and open range, this documentary delivers a sweeping view of the American West. Stream on Prime Video or watch for free on YouTube.

Read the Landscape

Desert heat, mountain streams, and wide-open skies become characters of their own in these transporting stories from the American West.

Inland

by Téa Obreht

In the drought-stricken Arizona Territory of 1893, frontierswoman Nora waits for her missing family while former outlaw Lurie sets out on an extraordinary journey haunted by restless spirits. Téa Obreht blends history, myth, and adventure into a sweeping reimagining of the American West.

The Guide

by Peter Heller

Jack takes a job at an exclusive fishing lodge tucked inside a secluded Colorado canyon, hoping that clear streams and mountain air will offer a fresh start. When a scream cuts through the night, his peaceful retreat becomes a tense wilderness mystery with something sinister hiding beneath the scenery.

Feel-good picks for living fully at every age

Hi, friend!

September is Healthy Aging Month, and we’re celebrating early by sharing stories that remind us there’s no deadline for finding joy, chasing a dream, or beginning again in our later years. From setting out on a long-awaited adventure to stepping back into the spotlight, these characters are making the most of every chapter. Read, watch, and let them inspire you to keep exploring what makes life meaningful.

It’s Never Too Late for a New Chapter

These spirited characters are setting out on long-awaited journeys, forging unexpected connections, and proving that some of life’s most meaningful adventures can begin later than planned.

Etta and Otto and Russell and James

by Emma Hooper

At 82, Etta leaves her farm and sets out on foot to see the ocean for the first time. Her remarkable journey across Canada becomes a moving exploration of memory, friendship, determination, and the dreams that stay with us until we’re finally ready to follow them.

Lillian Boxfish Takes a Walk

by Kathleen Rooney

On New Year’s Eve, 85-year-old Lillian Boxfish decides to trek across Manhattan, revisiting the places and memories that shaped her trailblazing career and eventful life. Witty, reflective, and full of personality, her walk becomes a celebration of independence, resilience, and finding delight in a city that keeps changing right alongside you.

Second Acts Worth Celebrating

Whether they’re returning to the stage or shaking up their routines, these characters discover that friendship, romance, creativity, and a little courage can make the next chapter every bit as exciting as the last.

Quartet

Streaming on Prime Video

At a retirement home for musicians, preparations for an annual concert get complicated when a celebrated opera singer—and plenty of unfinished history—arrives. Led by Maggie Smith, this warm comedy celebrates the joy of making music together at any age.

Book Club

Available to rent

Diane Keaton, Jane Fonda, Candice Bergen, and Mary Steenburgen star as four longtime friends whose monthly book club inspires them to shake up their relationships, routines, and expectations.

Still Stealing the Show

These sharp, funny shows prove that getting older doesn’t mean stepping out of the story.

Hacks

Streaming on HBO Max

Legendary comedian Deborah Vance refuses to let changing tastes—or anyone else—decide when her time in the spotlight is over. Her complicated partnership with a younger writer pushes both women to take creative risks, evolve, and discover that reinvention can be messy, hilarious, and deeply rewarding.

A Man on the Inside

Streaming on Netflix

Ted Danson stars as Charles, a retired widower who answers a private investigator’s ad and goes undercover at a retirement community. What begins as a secret assignment gives him a renewed sense of purpose, unexpected friendships, and a charming reminder that life can still surprise you when you decide to step back into it.

Shows to restore your faith in humanity

Hey, friend!

The Little League World Series is officially underway, which is the one moment every summer when our faith in humanity is collectively restored as we watch kids from different cultures around the world unite over competition and a love for baseball. In keeping with that theme, we've curated the best feel-good coming-of-age shows, the books that prove sports teach lessons no classroom ever could, and the underdog movies that need to be on your watchlist.

Coming-of-Age Shows to Restore Your Faith in Humanity

Nothing will make you optimistic for the future like watching teens overcoming adversity to become the best version of themselves. These are the series that do it best.

The Crossover

Twin basketball phenoms Josh and JB Bell are inseparable until growing up starts pulling them in different directions, on the court and off. Kwame Alexander adapts his own Newbery-winning novel, with Sean Patrick Thomas as their father, a former pro player adjusting to life after the NBA. It's the rare sports show that's also an uplifting family watch.

More Than a Game: Books About What Sports Actually Teach Us

In many of the best sports books, the game itself is almost beside the point. They use the sport as a way in, and what they're really writing about is everything that happens off the field.

The Art of Fielding

by Chad Harbach

Henry Skrimshander is a gifted shortstop who seems destined for big league stardom, until one wild throw shatters his confidence. Chad Harbach spent a decade writing his debut novel, which reads less like a sports book and more like a campus story about ambition, identity, and the fear of losing the one thing you counted on.

Long Shots: The Best Underdog Sports Movies

Everyone loves watching a team nobody believes in prove the haters wrong. Here are the underdog films you need to add to your watchlist.

The Mighty Ducks

A disgraced lawyer sentenced to community service must coach the worst pee-wee hockey team in Minnesota. Emilio Estevez spends the season turning a group of misfits who can't stay upright on skates into a team that actually believes in itself. It may not be a baseball movie, but it's the perfect story to pair with the Little League World Series.

posts.text:
What to watch, read, and shop for with your kids

Hi, friend!

Welcome back to Insider Pix, where we uncover what entertainment and culture insiders are watching, reading, and listening to! Next up:

Molly Patrick Epstein

Molly Patrick Epstein is the founder of Owl Tree, a secondhand kids’ and women’s business headquartered in Brooklyn. She is a native Texan, recovering corporate fashion merchant, and mom to 3 girls.

Molly’s 5 Picks

Best TV show you’ve watched recently?

I’ve been racing through Rivals! It’s great counterprogramming for parents after the kids go to bed. Think a re-imagining of a Rupert Murdoch-esque media titan, with terrific 80’s fashion, lots of sexy affairs, and a dive into British aristocracy via the Cotswolds. Very, very fun!

Best movie you watched recently?

We are having so much fun introducing our kids to stand-up comedy. John Mulaney's self-deprecating story-telling from his childhood and young adulthood, especially in The Comeback Kid & Kid Gorgeous, really hit! Sebastian Maniscalco’s misanthropic rants didn’t work as well with kids, so we’re now looking to try Nate Bargatze and Leanne Morgan as kid-friendly options. Nothing better than getting the giggles with your family.

A 5-star-worthy book you’d recommend to anyone?

On the heels of the Odyssey movie, if you haven’t read The Song of Achilles and Circe by Madeline Miller, I cannot recommend them more highly. Both novels are incredible re-tellings of ancient stories that set those story tropes entirely on their head.

I also just re-read The Hunger Games with my 11-year-old, and we were both racing to bedtime to pick back up each night, starting the 2nd book shortly. High recommendation for tweens & teens - the concept is dark, but the violence detail is minimal.

Go-to weekly podcast?

I listen to every Good Hang with Amy Poehler episode like I’m catching up with a close girlfriend. She’s a gracious, hilarious host and terrific interviewer, and as a fellow perimenopausal mother of teens, I find her framework for culture very relatable.

Pix: After 20 years in fashion retail, what did you know you wanted to do differently when you started Owl Tree?

“MPE: The kids’ market is the perfect use case for secondhand clothing. Kids outgrow things lightning-quick; they take terrible care of their clothes, and often have irrational taste preferences. Secondhand makes it less expensive and less precious for kids to find their self-expression! When I started, I didn’t think anyone was doing kids’ secondhand well. I’ve brought my full-price retail expertise and standards into a resale environment in our 2 Brooklyn stores & site, through curation, merchandising, customer service, and wardrobing. Eyeing locations now in Manhattan for our 3rd location!”

Pix: It’s back-to-school season! What advice do you have for parents shopping for a first-day-of-school outfit?

“MPE: As a mom of 3 kids, a critical lesson in everyone’s sanity is learning when to pick your battles. It may be disappointing that they don’t want to wear a polo collar or a twirly dress for their first day, but I also now kinda miss those kooky print mash-up outfits of the kindergarten years. As long as they are dressed sufficiently for the weather and won’t shock their grandma by what they’re wearing, I won't fight too hard and instead let their self-expression reign.

That said, if they did let me pick, for their first day I would make sure it’s seasonal for both early September weather and later on with sweaters & layers.”

Pix: What current fashion trend are you loving right now? And which would you like to permanently shelve?

“MPE: Isn’t it just delightful that women are no longer forced to wear uncomfortable heels to be fashionable? Ballet flats, loafers, & sleek low-heeled boots in classic leathers & suedes feel very modern again. Worn with soft neutral knits and 90’s silhouettes - it’s fabulous and a great time for all your classics to earn their keep. I’m going to pass on a Y2K revisit myself, and let my tweens & teens take on the low-rise denim, baby tees, and chokers.”

Pix: If you could swap closets with any TV or movie character whose wardrobe you still think about, who are you choosing?

“MPE: Hands down, it would be Rene Russo from The Thomas Crown Affair. Designed entirely by Michael Kors, every outfit she wears still feels sophisticated, sexy, and classic all at once.”

Pix: What’s the greatest secondhand score you’ve ever found?

“MPE: Ooh! I’m still buzzing from this one. This spring at a women’s consignment pop-up in Tribeca, I found a perfect-fitting, excellent-condition, current-season pair of chocolate brown Saint Laurent cargo pants for 1/8 of the retail price. I bought them and snuck out of the event quickly, feeling like I’d stolen treasure. We’ve just started selling women’s at Owl Tree, and I’m having so much fun getting deep into the women’s resale market now too!”

Nothing will make you optimistic for the future like watching teens overcoming adversity to become the best version of themselves. These are the series that do it best.

Hey, friend!

Did you know it’s currently Elvis Week? This annual week-long celebration of the “King of Rock & Roll” takes place every year in Memphis, Tennessee. Since most of us won’t be visiting the world-famous Graceland estate anytime soon, we decided to round up the best Elvis movies and docs, reads on rock 'n' roll's golden age, and the decade’s greatest musical biopics to help you celebrate from the comfort of your couch.

Long Live the King: The Best Elvis Movies & Docs

From the iconic sequined jumpsuits in Vegas to grainy archival footage of a 21-year-old kid at Sun Records, these are the movies and docs that show the man behind the music.

Elvis

Baz Luhrmann's fever-dream biopic tracks Elvis's rise and unraveling through the eyes of Colonel Tom Parker (Tom Hanks), the manager who built him into a phenomenon and profited off every moment of it. Austin Butler masterfully disappears into the role—so much so that his real-life voice still has hints of Elvis’s to this day.

Backstage Pass: Books Exploring the Golden Age of Rock 'n' Roll

Movies give you the highlight reel, but these books shine a light on everything that got left out: the label politics, the bad contracts, and the moments nobody put on film.

Last Train to Memphis

by Peter Guralnick

The first half of Peter Guralnick's two-volume Elvis biography covers his life from birth through 1958, before the Army, before Vegas, and before his songs took over the world. It's considered the definitive account of how rock 'n' roll began, treating Presley as a working musician rather than a myth.

Top 10 Musical Biopics of the Decade

Once Elvis Week comes to an end, here are 10 more must-watch musical biopics worth singing along to.

Respect

posts.title: Must-watch films to celebrate Elvis Week
posts.text:
Hey, friend!

Did you know it’s currently Elvis Week? This annual week-long celebration of the “King of Rock & Roll” takes place every year in Memphis, Tennessee. Since most of us won’t be visiting the world-famous Graceland estate anytime soon, we decided to round up the best Elvis movies and docs, reads on rock 'n' roll's golden age, and the decade’s greatest musical biopics to help you celebrate from the comfort of your couch.

Long Live the King: The Best Elvis Movies & Docs

From the iconic sequined jumpsuits in Vegas to grainy archival footage of a 21-year-old kid at Sun Records, these are the movies and docs that show the man behind the music.

Elvis

Baz Luhrmann's fever-dream biopic tracks Elvis's rise and unraveling through the eyes of Colonel Tom Parker (Tom Hanks), the manager who built him into a phenomenon and profited off every moment of it. Austin Butler masterfully disappears into the role—so much so that his real-life voice still has hints of Elvis’s to this day.

Backstage Pass: Books Exploring the Golden Age of Rock 'n' Roll

Movies give you the highlight reel, but these books shine a light on everything that got left out: the label politics, the bad contracts, and the moments nobody put on film.

Last Train to Memphis

by Peter Guralnick

The first half of Peter Guralnick's two-volume Elvis biography covers his life from birth through 1958, before the Army, before Vegas, and before his songs took over the world. It's considered the definitive account of how rock 'n' roll began, treating Presley as a working musician rather than a myth.

Top 10 Musical Biopics of the Decade

Once Elvis Week comes to an end, here are 10 more must-watch musical biopics worth singing along to.

Respect

Aretha Franklin handpicked Jennifer Hudson to play her years before this film got made, and it's easy to see why once Hudson opens her mouth. The story tracks Franklin's rise from her father's church choir to international stardom.

posts.title: “An epic love story... a gorgeously written novel”
posts.text:
Hi, friend!

Welcome back to Insider Pix, where we uncover what entertainment and culture insiders are watching, reading, and listening to! Next up:

Leigh Haber

Leigh Haber is a seasoned publishing executive who spent a decade overseeing Oprah’s Book Club and book coverage for O Magazine and Oprah Daily, where she served as VP, Books. Her wide-ranging career has included roles as an editor, publicity director, producer, speechwriter, and book reviewer, and she has worked with authors including Al Gore, Steve Martin, Terry Gross, and Alice Walker. She now joins Sourcebooks as VP, Executive Director of Communications and Special Projects.

Leigh’s 5 Picks

A 5-star-worthy book you’d recommend to anyone?

The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny by Kiran Desai. Yes, it’s 700-something pages, but it’s an epic love story alongside a portrait of alienation and displacement—a gorgeously written novel by the Booker Prize-winning author of The Inheritance of Loss.

Best TV show you’ve watched recently?

It’s a tie between Hacks and The Comeback. Hacks is hilarious—the relationship between its two stars is so complex and electric. Jean Smart is a genius. And The Comeback is off-kilter in a way that is so Lisa Kudrow. Riveting.

Best movie you watched recently?

Michael, starring Jaafar Jackson. I know there will be haters for this choice, but I couldn’t take my eyes off the screen. Jaafar’s performance was off the charts, and I’d forgotten how great the music is.

A hidden gem you wish more people knew about?

The film Juliet, Naked. Starring Rose Byrne, Ethan Hawke, and Chris O’Dowd—I love its quirky warmth.

Go-to weekly podcast?

Good Hang with Amy Poehler. She’s like the embodiment of fun. Takes me out of my head. That episode with Will Ferrell?? Awkward and hilarious.

Pix: What is the best book you’ve read so far this year, and what made it stand out?

“LH: It’s a tie between The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout and Whistler by Ann Patchett. I didn’t want either of them to end.”

Pix: You spent over a decade as the Director of Oprah’s Book Club. Is there a particular Oprah's Book Club selection or author that holds a special place in your heart, and what makes it so memorable?

“LH: I can narrow it down to three. An American Marriage by Tayari Jones is one. I’d loved Tayari’s Silver Sparrow but wasn’t able to get Oprah to select it, so when An American Marriage came out, I was all over it. And Tayari is a delight. We picked The Underground Railroad by Colson Whitehead, and that was before he won the Pulitzer. Very proud of that one. And then Caste by Isabel Wilkerson. I think those who read it with us began to view racism in a completely different way.”

Pix: If you could host a dream dinner party with three authors—dead or alive—who's getting an invitation and why?

“LH: Toni Morrison, for sure. I adore her fiction, but she was also such a great essayist and thinker. She would preside over the dinner party, in my fantasy. (and of course Oprah did hold a dinner party on camera with her…) Amor Towles would have to be there, because he’s such a classic gentleman and I love his white suits. And I’d have to go with Toni Cade Bambara as our third. She and Toni were friends and colleagues, and TCB is such an underrated writer. She also had a sparkling personality–radiated warmth and humor.”

Pix: You are the director of The Ink Book Club, which has a call to action for all bibliophiles: “In this era of book banning, be fierce!” If you could put a banned book into every reader’s hands, which would you pick and why?

“LH: The 1619 Project, by Nikole Hannah-Jones. We have to start looking at our country’s history more realistically if we are going to move forward in a productive way.”

The most chilling true crime shows of 2026 — Today's Pix

Earlier this summer, Netflix's Maternal Instinct had everyone talking about its chilling depiction of a real COVID-era case. Now, a new season of Conversations with a Killer is landing this week. With the genre having a killer lineup this summer, we've rounded up the most fascinating true crime stories across TV, podcasts, and books.

THE MOST CHILLING TRUE CRIME SHOWS OF THE YEAR (SO FAR)
True crime TV isn't just popular right now, it's absolutely dominating. These are the new shows that made viewers stay up way past their bedtime, one creepy episode at a time.
Conversations with a Killer: The Charles Manson Tapes — Joe Berlinger's docuseries returns for a new volume, tracing Charles Manson's rise as a cult leader through unreleased prison recordings, firsthand accounts, and archival footage most viewers have never seen. It's the franchise's darkest season yet, and the closest anyone's gotten to hearing Manson explain himself in his own words. Only on Netflix August 12.

NEW & UNSETTLING TRUE CRIME PODCASTS
From mysterious cold cases to shocking family secrets nobody saw coming, the best true crime podcasts of the year prove the genre still has new angles to explore.
The Idiot — For years, M. Gessen wrote about the world's worst people: dictators, terrorists, human rights abusers. Then their own cousin Allen got arrested for trying to have his ex-wife killed. Serial Productions' latest is the studio's funniest true crime podcast yet, and its most personal.

PAGE-TURNERS: THE MOST ADDICTIVE TRUE CRIME BOOKS OF 2026
The best true crime writing turns real tragedy into something you can't put down without ever losing the human stakes.
London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe — Patrick Radden Keefe, the writer behind Say Nothing and Empire of Pain, tells the story of a London teenager who invented an entire identity as a Russian oligarch's son before he was found dead in the Thames. This devastating and spellbinding read is easily one of the biggest books of the year.

posts.text:
Olivie Blake's latest is "a gory, gothic masterpiece" — Book Pix
By Genevieve, Books Content Manager @ Pix

August is kind of a weird month: summer isn't over, fall hasn't started, and everyone is scrambling to take a few more days of vacation. So why not lean into the weirdness? Today's books are delightfully off-kilter, with a bloody Hollywood tale, some multiverse romance, and more.

FANTASY SPOTLIGHT — Dreamland by Olivie Blake
New York Times bestselling author Olivie Blake (The Atlas Six, Girl Dinner) returns with a bloody good novel about an aspiring actress who is drawn into the orbit of a powerful Hollywood dynasty, as a seductive heir and her own ambition threaten to consume her. Alix E. Harrow (Starling House) raves: "This is Olivie Blake at the height of her power, doing cartwheels on the high wire. Dreamland is a sweat-slick Hollywood fable about fame, fortune, and the sins we'd commit for either. A gory, gothic masterpiece."

ROMANCE SPOTLIGHT — In What World by Bridget Morrissey
In this "true love letter to theatre kids and queer folks" (Hannah Bonam-Young), two former high school rivals begrudgingly reunite to find their missing drama teacher, only to tumble through a series of alternate realities where other versions of themselves are much more honest about their feelings for each other. Equal parts multiverse adventure and simmering second-chance romance, this clever, heartfelt novel asks what happens when the person you can't stand might be the person you can't live without.

THE REVIEWS ARE IN
"A tour de force." —The Atlantic
"A rare and beautifully controlled novel of magic, intrigue, and obsession…. Delightful and dangerous. A feat of marvelous showmanship!" —Rachel Beanland, author of This House Is on Fire
"One of the most unusual, thought-provoking books you'll read this year." —BookPage

As my colleagues and I cackled over all the early Wicker memes, I felt the need to point out that sentient object smut is an actual romance subgenre. And just like Wicker, they frequently serve a hefty dose of humor along with their spice.
Unhinged by Vera Valentine — In this paranormal romance, a woman must trust the sentient front door that's secretly protected her for years when a deadly stalker threatens her life. As odd as it may sound, this book has a cult following: more than 10k reviews on Amazon and almost 30k on Goodreads. The door is actually a dryad shifter who gets stuck in door form, so there's a Greek mythology angle. Readers agree it is totally bonkers, yet somehow completely delightful.

THE BIG DEBUT — The Responsible Party by Claire Carusillo
When a modern-day scandal and a decades-old murder collide, a canceled skincare influencer uncovers the wild history of the "unsinkable" women who came before her. Vulture calls this debut about an unforgettable family "pleasurably busy and delightfully odd," while The New York Times hails it as "a rollicking, hilarious tale of shipwreck, shenanigans and murder."

THRILLER SPOTLIGHT — The Secrets We Hide by Karin Slaughter
Sheriff Clifton is back in the next North Falls mystery from #1 New York Times bestselling author Karin Slaughter, the powerhouse behind The Good Daughter and the Will Trent series. Expect buried secrets, mounting suspicions, and plenty of twists as Clifton and her sister unravel what really happened to the Vickery family one terrible night. Freida McFadden: "Few writers can balance pulse-pounding suspense and emotional truth as brilliantly as Karin Slaughter."

PAGE TO SCREEN — My Brilliant Career
A 125-year-old novel is getting a very 2026 glow-up. Premiering August 13 on Netflix, My Brilliant Career gives Miles Franklin's 1901 classic a wildly modern makeover, following aspiring writer Sybylla Melvyn (Philippa Northeast) as she chooses creative ambition over marriage and society's expectations in early 20th-century Australia. Created by an all-female team of writers, producers, and directors.

BOOKWORLD
Barack Obama is launching a podcast about his favorite books. This poet has a powerful idea about what reading can do. Heated Rivalry has cast its Troy and Harris.
Guess the Book answer: Verity by Colleen Hoover — the adaptation starring Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, and Josh Hartnett is less than two months away.

Author Spotlight

Oliver Burkeman is a British journalist and author known for challenging productivity, time management, and self-improvement culture. His writing blends psychology, philosophy, and humor to help readers make peace with their limitations during trying times rather than constantly trying to push past them.

Four Thousand Weeks

When summer feels like an overwhelming marathon of events, Burkeman offers relief: you were never meant to do it all. Reach for this guide when the FOMO gets loud—it's a quiet, steadying reminder that missing a few pool days won't cost you the meaningful life you're after.

Meditations for Mortals

This national bestseller is built for the days when your motivation is low or you’re stuck inside. These bite-sized daily reflections meet you where you are, no big life overhaul required. Think of it as your “OK” to let today just be what it is.

Great Escapes Indoors

Enjoy wellness tips and entertainment in your home by putting on a docuseries that takes you to far-off places.

Streaming on Netflix

Explorer Dan Buettner travels to the world's longest-living communities — from Sardinia to Okinawa — uncovering the diet, movement, and social habits behind their longevity, and distilling his findings into lessons anyone can apply.

Ten Percent Happier
